A1.title: Very Hot Days in America and Europe
A1.content:
It is summer now. The weather is very hot. In the east of the United States, it is very, very hot this week. Many cities have hot days. The sun is strong. The air is heavy. People feel tired. It is hard to work outside.

This is a heat wave. A heat wave is many hot days together. The heat wave is in big cities like New York and Washington. It is also in small towns. Weather experts say the heat can be dangerous. Old people and small children must be careful. Sick people must be careful too.

What can people do? They can drink a lot of water. They can stay inside. They can use a fan or air conditioning. They should not run or play sports in the afternoon. The afternoon is the hottest time. The morning and the evening are better. People should wear light clothes. They should also help their neighbors. Some old people live alone. A friendly visit can save a life.

Europe is also very hot. A big heat wave moved across Europe. Many countries had record heat. A record means the highest number ever. Some cities in Europe were hotter than ever before. The heat wave is now moving east. It goes to new countries. People in Europe also need to drink water and stay cool. Some schools close early. Some trains go slowly because the rails get too hot.

Why is it so hot? Weather experts say summers are getting hotter in many places. Hot days come earlier. Heat waves stay longer. This is a big problem for cities. Cities are hotter than the countryside. Buildings and roads hold the heat. At night, cities do not cool down fast.

Doctors have simple advice. First, drink water many times every day. Do not wait until you are thirsty. Second, stay out of the sun from noon to four in the afternoon. Third, keep your home cool. Close the windows in the day. Open them at night. Fourth, check on family and friends. A short phone call is good.

Hot weather is also hard for workers. Farmers work in the sun. Builders work in the sun too. Some companies change work hours. People start early in the morning. They rest in the hot afternoon. This keeps workers safe.

The heat will not stop soon. Weather experts say more hot days are coming. This weekend may be very hot again. In America, July 4 is a holiday. Many people go outside for the holiday. They watch fireworks. They have picnics. Experts say: have fun, but be careful. Find shade. Drink water. Rest often.

Hot weather is part of summer. But very hot weather can hurt people. Simple actions keep us safe. Water, shade, and rest are the three big helpers. Remember them this summer, in America, in Europe, and everywhere.

vocabulary.definition: many very hot days that come together
the highest or best number ever
a cool place out of the sun
a person who knows a lot about something
not safe; it can hurt you

A2.title: Taiwan's First Space Telescope Reaches Orbit
A2.content:
Taiwan has good news from space. The island's first space telescope is now in orbit around the Earth. This is a big moment for Taiwan's science and technology. Many people worked on the project for years, and now their machine is flying high above the planet.

A space telescope is a special camera that looks at stars, planets, and galaxies. It is different from a telescope on the ground. On the ground, clouds and city lights make it hard to see the sky clearly. In space, there are no clouds and no lights. So a space telescope can take much clearer pictures.

The telescope traveled into space on a rocket. After the launch, engineers waited for a signal. When the signal came, they knew the telescope was safe and working. The team was very happy. Scientists in Taiwan will now test all the parts. First they check the power system. Then they check the cameras. After the tests, the telescope can start its real work.

Why is this important for Taiwan? Taiwan is famous for making computer chips. Companies around the world use chips from Taiwan. But Taiwan also wants to grow its space industry. A space program needs many skills: building satellites, writing software, and studying data. These skills can help students find good jobs in the future.

The project also helps education. Teachers can use the telescope's pictures in class. Students can learn about stars and space weather. Some universities in Taiwan will study the data together. Young scientists can join real space research without leaving home. This was not possible before.

Space is becoming important for many countries in Asia. Japan, India, and South Korea all have space programs. Now Taiwan is joining this group with its own telescope. Working in space also means working with other countries. Scientists often share their results, so one small telescope can help researchers everywhere.

There were problems along the way. Building a space telescope is very hard. The parts must be light but strong. They must work in extreme cold and heat. The team tested everything many times. Sometimes tests failed, and the engineers had to fix the design. But they did not give up.

What happens next? In the coming weeks, the telescope will send its first pictures back to Earth. Scientists call this moment 'first light.' It is like opening your eyes for the first time. Everyone is waiting for these first images. If all goes well, the telescope will work for several years.

This story shows that a small place can do big things. Taiwan is not a large country, but it has strong engineers and scientists. The new telescope is a symbol of that strength. Many students watched the launch online. Maybe some of them will build the next telescope. For now, Taiwan can look up at the night sky and know that its own eyes are up there, looking back at the stars.

vocabulary.definition: the path of an object as it moves around the Earth or another body in space
a tool that makes far-away things look bigger and clearer
the moment when a rocket leaves the ground and goes to space
a message sent by radio or electronic means
a machine that moves around the Earth in space

B1.title: Japan Protests Chinese Coast Guard Activity Near Yonaguni
B1.content:
Japan has made a formal protest to China because of Chinese coast guard activity near Yonaguni, a small Japanese island that lies just east of Taiwan. Japan's Chief Cabinet Secretary, Kihara Minoru, called the maritime activity 'unacceptable' and said that Japan would continue to watch the situation closely.

Yonaguni is Japan's westernmost island. It is only about 110 kilometers from Taiwan, so anything that happens in the waters around it matters to both Japan and Taiwan. In recent years, Chinese coast guard ships have appeared more and more often in this area. Although these ships belong to the coast guard and not the navy, they are large, well-equipped, and often stay near disputed waters for days at a time.

Why does this matter? First, the area is important for trade. Many cargo ships pass through the waters between Taiwan and Japan every day. If there is tension in these waters, shipping could become slower and more expensive. Second, the area is important for security. Japan worries that China is trying to change the situation in the region step by step, without starting an open conflict. Each new patrol pushes a little further than the last one.

Japan has responded in several ways. The government sent its protest through diplomatic channels, which is the normal first step. In addition, Japan has been strengthening its defenses on its southwestern islands, including Yonaguni, where it has built radar stations and placed small military units. Japan is also working more closely with partners such as the United States, Australia, and the Philippines.

China, on the other hand, says that its coast guard is carrying out normal duties in waters that it claims. Chinese officials often argue that Japan is exaggerating the problem. However, neighboring countries see a clear pattern: more ships, more flights, and more pressure in the East China Sea and around Taiwan.

For Taiwan, this news is significant because it shows how connected the region's security has become. When Chinese ships operate near Yonaguni, they are also operating near Taiwan. Experts say that Japan and Taiwan share an interest in keeping the seas open and peaceful. Recently, Japan has also increased economic cooperation with Taiwan and India, for example through a new 'digital corridor' project that supports technology partnerships.

What could happen next? Most experts do not expect a sudden crisis. Instead, they expect more of the same: patrols, protests, and careful watching from all sides. Still, there is a risk that a small accident at sea could grow into a bigger problem, especially if ships come too close to each other.

In short, the protest over Yonaguni is one more sign of rising tension in East Asia. Japan wants to defend its islands without making the situation worse, while China continues to expand its presence at sea. The rest of the region, including Taiwan, is watching carefully, because peace in these waters is important for everyone's safety and trade.

vocabulary.definition: an official statement saying that you strongly disagree with something
government ships and officers that watch and control a country's coastal waters
connected with the sea or ships
the act of moving around an area to watch or guard it
a situation in which people or countries feel stress and distrust toward each other

B2.title: US and Iran Report 'Positive Progress' in Indirect Doha Talks
B2.content:
Indirect talks between the United States and Iran wrapped up in Doha this week, with Qatar, the host and mediator, describing the discussions as having made 'positive progress.' The talks were held at a lower level than earlier rounds, with messages passed between the two delegations through Qatari mediators rather than face to face. Modest as that may sound, any progress is notable given the violence that has marked recent months.

The backdrop to these negotiations is a war that has already cost the United States tens of billions of dollars and has repeatedly threatened to spiral into a wider regional conflict. Following American strikes on targets in Iran earlier this summer and an agreement signed in June, the two sides have been trying to stabilize a fragile ceasefire while accusing each other of violating its terms. Diplomacy has continued in fits and starts, and the Doha channel is currently the most active line of communication between Washington and Tehran.

The timing of the latest round is particularly sensitive. Iran is preparing to hold a multi-day funeral for its slain supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, with ceremonies planned from July 4 through July 9 in locations across Iran and Iraq. Iranian negotiators have now left Doha as the country pauses its diplomacy ahead of the funeral. President Masoud Pezeshkian has urged Iranians to attend in large numbers, and Iran's army has warned the United States and Israel against launching any attacks during the processions. In other words, the region is holding its breath: a week of mourning could either calm the situation or provide a spark for new escalation.

Meanwhile, tensions remain high in the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil passes. Iran issued a fresh warning this week for vessels to follow Tehran-designated routes through the strait, a move that many shipping companies see as an attempt to demonstrate control over the waterway. Insurance costs for tankers have risen, and energy analysts warn that fuel prices could climb further if the situation deteriorates.

What does 'positive progress' actually mean in this context? Diplomats caution that it does not signal a breakthrough. Rather, it suggests that both sides are still willing to talk, that the ceasefire, however imperfect, is worth preserving, and that mediators like Qatar retain the trust of both capitals. For Washington, continued talks offer a path to avoid another costly military campaign. For Tehran, negotiating during a leadership transition allows it to project stability at a moment of deep uncertainty.

The coming days will be a test. If the funeral period passes without violence, talks are expected to resume, possibly at a higher level. If not, the fragile diplomatic thread could snap. Observers around the world, from oil traders to foreign ministries, will be watching Iran closely this week, aware that events there can quickly ripple outward into the global economy and international security.

vocabulary.definition: a person or country that helps two opposing sides communicate and reach agreement
an agreement to stop fighting, usually temporarily
an increase in the intensity or seriousness of a conflict
a group of people chosen to represent a country or organization in talks
to become worse over time

C1.title: Mourning and Maneuvering: Iran Pauses Diplomacy to Bury Khamenei
C1.content:
Iran stands at one of the most consequential junctures in its post-revolutionary history. As the Islamic Republic prepares a multi-day funeral for its slain supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, the machinery of diplomacy has been deliberately suspended: Iranian negotiators have departed Doha, where indirect talks with the United States had been quietly inching forward under Qatari mediation. The ceremonies, scheduled from July 4 through July 9 and spanning sites in both Iran and Iraq, will be far more than a religious observance. They will function as a demonstration of state cohesion, a test of public sentiment, and a stage upon which the Islamic Republic's next chapter begins to take shape.

The official choreography is already apparent. President Masoud Pezeshkian has appealed to Iranians to attend the funeral 'in large numbers' — a request that reveals the government's anxiety as much as its ambition. A massive turnout would allow the leadership to claim popular legitimacy at a moment of acute vulnerability; a sparse one would broadcast weakness to adversaries abroad and rivals within. Simultaneously, the army's warning to the United States and Israel against launching attacks during the processions underscores how thin the margin for miscalculation has become. In effect, Tehran is asking for a truce of respect while implicitly conceding that it fears the funeral could present a tempting window for its enemies.

The diplomatic context adds another layer of complexity. Qatar characterized the just-concluded round of indirect talks as having achieved 'positive progress' — carefully calibrated language that acknowledges movement without promising resolution. The talks themselves were conducted at a lower level than previous rounds, suggesting both sides wished to keep expectations modest while preserving the channel. For Washington, the calculus involves balancing pressure against the risk of reigniting a war that has already, by the Pentagon's own accounting, consumed tens of billions of dollars. For Tehran's interim power brokers, negotiation offers breathing room, but any visible concession during a period of mourning risks accusations of betrayal from hardliners eager to define the succession on their own terms.

Beyond the negotiating table, Iran continues to wield its geographic leverage. This week it renewed warnings that commercial vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz should follow Tehran-designated routes — an assertion of authority over a waterway carrying roughly one-fifth of global oil flows. The move serves multiple purposes: it reminds Western capitals of Iran's capacity to disrupt the global economy, reassures domestic audiences that the state remains potent despite decapitation of its leadership, and establishes bargaining chips for future talks.

What follows the funeral will reveal much. Succession in the Islamic Republic is not merely a personnel question; it is a referendum on the system's direction — whether toward pragmatic accommodation or defiant retrenchment. The composition of mourning crowds, the tenor of official rhetoric, and the speed with which negotiators return to Doha will offer early indications. For now, the region inhabits a suspended moment: a pause that is neither peace nor war, in which grief, power, and strategy are inseparably intertwined.

vocabulary.definition: a particular and often critical point in time or in a series of events
the condition of being accepted as rightful and valid, especially regarding political authority
carefully adjusted or measured to achieve a precise effect
the process by which one leader or authority replaces another
a retreat to a more defensive or conservative position

C2.title: Confidence Amid Contest: Taiwan's Economic Poise in a Region Under Strain
C2.content:
There is a quietly instructive dissonance in this week's news from East Asia. On one hand, Taiwan's consumer confidence rose in June, buoyed — according to survey researchers — by easing geopolitical tensions and lower energy prices. On the other, Japan lodged a formal protest over Chinese coast guard operations near Yonaguni, its westernmost island, barely a hundred kilometers from Taiwan's coast, with Chief Cabinet Secretary Kihara Minoru branding the activity 'unacceptable.' That consumers can grow more sanguine even as gray-zone pressure intensifies offshore is not a paradox so much as a portrait of how societies habituate to protracted, sub-threshold coercion.

The confidence data merit scrutiny beyond the headline. Sentiment indices are as much psychological artifacts as economic ones; they register not objective risk but perceived trajectory. June's improvement likely reflects the tentative de-escalation in the Middle East, where a fragile US-Iran ceasefire and renewed indirect talks in Doha have taken some of the fever out of global energy markets. For an island that imports the overwhelming share of its energy, softer oil prices translate directly into household purchasing power and industrial margins. Taiwan's export machine, meanwhile, continues to ride the artificial intelligence boom: EVA Air's cargo revenues are surging on AI-related demand, and the semiconductor supply chain remains the indispensable substrate of the global technology economy.

Yet the security backdrop refuses to recede. The Yonaguni protest exemplifies a pattern that scholars of coercive statecraft would recognize instantly: the incremental normalization of presence. Coast guard vessels, nominally civilian instruments of law enforcement, probe contested waters with a persistence calculated to fall below any threshold that would justify a forceful response. Each sortie recalibrates the baseline; yesterday's provocation becomes today's routine. Japan's countermeasures — radar installations, garrisons on its southwestern arc, deepened alignment with Washington, Canberra, and Manila — represent the mirror-image logic of deterrence by accumulation.

Taiwan occupies the geometric and strategic center of this contest, and its responses have been characteristically multidimensional. Taipei recently flagged China's Amap navigation platform over allegedly excessive data uploads, a reminder that the contest extends into the digital substrate of everyday life. Tokyo's newly launched 'digital corridor' with Taiwan and India signals an emergent architecture of technological alignment among democracies wary of dependence on Chinese infrastructure. Even the successful orbiting of Taiwan's first space telescope, ostensibly a purely scientific milestone, carries strategic connotations: space capability is dual-use by nature, and indigenous aerospace competence enhances resilience.

The deeper question is whether economic self-assurance and strategic anxiety can coexist indefinitely, or whether one must eventually subordinate the other. History offers ambiguous counsel. Societies under sustained pressure sometimes fracture; more often, they adapt, pricing risk into daily life with remarkable equanimity. Taiwan's citizens, surveyed in June, evidently judged the immediate horizon brighter than the recent past. Whether that judgment proves prescient or premature will depend on variables largely beyond their control: the durability of the Middle Eastern ceasefire, the trajectory of Chinese assertiveness, and the steadfastness of allied commitments. For now, confidence itself is a form of quiet defiance — and perhaps the most rational posture available.

vocabulary.definition: a lack of agreement or harmony between things, ideas, or impressions
optimistic or positive, especially in a difficult situation
describing coercive actions that fall between normal peacetime behavior and open warfare
mental calmness and composure, especially under stress
having accurate knowledge or judgment of events before they happen
